content: Rhamnose is a naturally occurring sugar that lacks one oxygen atom, classifying it as a deoxy sugar. It can be further categorized as either a methyl-pentose or a 6-deoxy-hexose, depending on its structural characteristics. In nature, rhamnose predominantly exists in its L-form, specifically as L-rhamnose, also known as 6-deoxy-L-mannose. This is notable because most naturally occurring sugars are found in the D-form. However, there are exceptions to this rule, including the methyl-pentoses L-fucose and L-rhamnose, as well as the pentose L-arabinose. L-Rhamnose can be extracted from plants such as Buckthorn (genus Rhamnus) and poison sumac. Additionally, it is present in the form of glycosides in a wide variety of other plant species. Beyond its presence in plants, rhamnose is a critical component of the outer cell membrane of acid-fast bacteria belonging to the Mycobacterium genus. This genus includes Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the pathogen responsible for causing tuberculosis.
